1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Tartakower Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..background: Also known as the Korchnoi Variation: Viktor Korchnoi played it many times, including in his first world championship match with Anatoly Karpov, and Ulf Andersson has also employed it.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..strategy: Supports d4 and gives the queen the c2 square, so White keeps a solid centre and the better structure. With the bishop coming to d3, White plays for a lasting edge against the doubled pawns without taking risks.

Puts the bishop on its active diagonal at once, looking at f7, instead of supporting d4 first. Black answers with normal development, and White's structural edge is no quicker to reach, so it is a sound, less common way to play for a small advantage.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Forgacs Variation

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..strategy: Develops the bishop to its best square: it covers the kingside, eyes h2 and prepares castling. Black accepts the doubled pawns for a harmonious position and uses the open lines for piece play, which is the point of the line.
